newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Forecasts for SIA cut on poor half-year.
newsitem.headline: Forecasts for SIA cut on poor half-year.

text.p: Singapore Airlines' (SIA) net profit may fall year-on-year in 1996/97 after it turned in disappointing half-year results, analysts said on Monday.
The national carrier earlier announced a modest 7.2 percent rise in net profit to Singapore $560.5 million (US$397.5 million) for the six months to September 30, from S$522.7 million the year before.
The result was towards the bottom of market expectations, which had ranged from S$550 million to over S$600 million.
Group operating profit fell 11.4 percent to S$467.6 million and the net result was only saved by a contribution of S$122.7 million from the sale of aircraft and spare parts, SIA said.
"We have to revise down our forecasts for the full-year," said Lim Eng Hai, head of research at brokerage J.M. Sassoon.
"The results were disappointing all round."
Several analysts said SIA may not even make the S$1.00 billion mark in 1996/97. It reported a net profit of S$1.025 billion in 1995/96.
SIA's share price fell more than five percent in early trading on Monday after the results were released, with the company's foreign share tranche down 80 cents to S$13.20.
SIA's results statement said the airline had benefited from an increase in passenger traffic, which had helped push up group revenue by 4.6 percent to S$3.53 billion from S$3.37 billion.
It carried 5.93 million passengers in the six months to September 30, up 10.2 percent from the same period in 1995. Total cargo rose 10.5 percent to 320,900 tonnes from 290,500 tonnes.
But the company said it had been buffeted by escalating jet fuel prices and the strength of the Singapore dollar, eroding its operating yield by 6.7 percent.
And it expected yields to continue to come under pressure during the second half of the year.

"While there may be some respite on the currency front, the direction of fuel prices in the second half is uncertain, as is the recovery of the cargo market," it quoted deputy chairman and chief executive officer Cheong Choong Kong as saying.

Analysts agreed jet fuel prices would continue to be a problem for SIA but said the main challenge would be increasing competition for passengers, particularly for those travelling economy class on the most popular routes.
"It's tough," said Neil Payne, head of research at ING Barings. "Some other carriers have been cutting fares and I don't see SIA being able to put up its prices to cover costs."
"Escalating costs and falling yields suggest the full-year will be difficult," he added.
Analysts noted that SIA said it would not be able to repeat in the second half the one-off gain it made from selling old aircraft and spares in the first-half.
ING Barings now believes SIA's year net will be around S$941 million for the year ending March 31, 1997, down eight percent.
Most previous forecasts showed a rise of 14 percent to around S$1.16 billion for 1996/97, the Estimate Directory shows.

Several other brokerages said they were planning to cut their full-year forecasts to around or slightly below S$1.00 billion, implying falls of between two and three percent, but said they were not yet ready to publish their forecasts.
